messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ryan was twenty-one, a former infantryman who now drove a city bus through the same downtown streets he had first navigated as a frightened teenager. Two years earlier, in the Helmand province, he had been riding in the lead Humvee of a supply convoy when a roadside IED detonated directly beneath them. The blast had been a single, deafening crack that tore through the vehicle in a sickening ripple. Flames erupted from the engine block, filling the crew compartment with the acrid, greasy smell of burning rubber and diesel. His buddy, seated to his left, was killed instantly, his body thrown against the radio mount. Ryan had been pulled from the wreckage by the medic and loaded onto a medevac helicopter, the rotor blades thumping a frantic rhythm against the heat-hazed sky. That was the last thing he remembered clearly; everything after came in disconnected pieces—the sound of the explosion reverberating inside his skull, the burnt smell clinging to his uniform, the helicopter’s blades, but never a coherent story he could put into words. He knew what had happened, but when he tried to describe it, the words simply would not come.

Back home, Ryan’s world had shrunk. He had come to believe that every street corner, every passing car, every closed space could hold another threat. The world no longer felt neutral—it felt actively dangerous, and he had to be on guard all the time. That hypervigilance bled into everything. Because he was certain that a crowd could mask a bomber or a sudden noise could signal an ambush, he avoided shopping centres and public events entirely. What frightened him most was the thought that he might let his guard down. He also stopped going to church, a place he had once found comfort; now it felt hollow, and he was not sure his life was worth living anymore anyway. To keep the thoughts at bay, he spent long hours on his phone, scrolling through social media or playing endless rounds of a mobile game, sometimes until three in the morning. If he was not driving or sleeping, he was escaping into the screen.

The memories of that day never stayed away for long. They came in disjointed fragments—the blast, the flame, the helicopter—playing over and over like a film stuck on repeat. When the replay would start, he would instantly pull out his phone, thumb jabbing at the screen to drown the images in distraction. But the more he used his phone to push the memories aside, the more those memories seemed to return in disconnected pieces, as if his avoidance had shattered them further. And each intrusive replay reinforced his conviction that the world was a dangerous place designed to take him by surprise.

His daily life as a bus driver put him directly in contact with his triggers. One afternoon, a truck on the freeway backfired with a sharp bang; Ryan’s hands locked on the steering wheel and he had to pull over, the explosion memory flooding back with the same sickening clarity. Another time, a passenger’s burnt toast from a bag nearby released a faint smoky smell, and for a moment he was back in the burning Humvee. Helicopters passing overhead during his shift made his jaw clench, the rotor sound pinching something deep in his chest. His hypervigilance only worsened after each trigger, convincing him he could never feel safe.

The self-reinforcing loop tightened. His belief that life was no longer worth living made the memory feel like a punishment he deserved, locking it in replay. The avoidance he used to escape the memory only ensured it stayed fragmented and vivid. Month after month, Ryan became more isolated. He had stopped seeing friends, and his supervisor had warned him about his erratic reactions during shifts. What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning when he saw a military-style helmet in a passenger’s lap and, for a split second, the world dissolved into the smell of diesel and the thud of rotors. He knew he could not keep driving away from it. He wanted the memories to stop, but deep down he was terrified that nothing would ever make them quiet.
